headline: Venezuela's interim president says the US oil agreement runs 25 years, not the 100 Washington describes
dek: Delcy Rodriguez told Venezuelans at the weekend that the country keeps ownership of its resources. US officials have briefed a 100-year development right and a 55 per cent share of output from the same fields.
summary: Venezuela's interim president says the oil agreement announced by Donald Trump lasts 25 years and leaves ownership in Venezuelan hands, an account that differs from the one US officials have given.

body.text: Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, said in a televised address at the weekend that the oil agreement announced by US President Donald Trump on Friday will run for 25 years and leaves Venezuela's ownership of its own resources intact. That is not the account US officials have given. Briefing the Associated Press, they described a new company holding **100-year** rights to develop the same 17 oil fields, with 55 per cent of the effective output going to the United States. Neither government has published the text of the agreement.

Trump announced the deal in a social media post on Friday, saying it had been negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth with Rodriguez. Rodriguez has led the government in Caracas since January, when US forces took the then president, Nicolas Maduro, out of the country in a night raid; he is awaiting trial in New York on drug- and weapons-related charges. The White House has said little about the agreement beyond Trump's post, according to the Associated Press.
The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!
body.cite: Donald Trump, US president, in a social media post, via ABC (Australia)

body.text: Two accounts of the same agreement

On the American account, reported by the Associated Press and attributed to unnamed US officials, a company formed by the US government and an unnamed private operator would hold 100-year development rights over 17 fields containing 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. The 55 per cent figure is described as "effective output" — a combination of an ownership stake and a right to buy oil at cost — with the crude going to the US strategic reserve and to the military. Officials said the company would be the second largest oil producer after Saudi Aramco. The private partner has not been identified.

Rodriguez's account describes the same 17 fields and the same 65 billion barrels, but a 25-year bilateral project with an initial production target of more than 1.5 million barrels a day, eight new blocks, and $19 from every barrel produced and sold to the United States flowing to Caracas. The money figures also differ between reports. The Associated Press, citing a Venezuelan government statement, gives $100 billion of investment and more than $209 billion in tax revenue for Caracas. Al Jazeera, reporting on Sunday, describes the $209 billion as what the arrangement could be worth to Venezuela **per year**, depending on oil prices. Agency copy carried by Daily Sabah puts the promised tax revenue at more than $204 billion. None of these has been reconciled by either government.
One thing must be absolutely clear: Venezuela retains ownership and sovereignty over its resources.
body.cite: Delcy Rodriguez, interim president of Venezuela, via Daily Sabah

body.text: Venezuela holds the largest known crude deposit in the world — about 303 billion barrels of proven reserves, roughly 17 per cent of global supply — but produces around 1 per cent of the world's oil. The gap is infrastructure. The Associated Press reports that the country once produced more than 2.5 million barrels a day above its current level, and that its oil installations are dilapidated after years of underinvestment and sanctions. No source consulted gave a current daily output figure.
It's going to take time — many years — to deploy that much capital and produce the kind of incremental results that history suggests possible.
body.cite: Kevin Book, managing director, ClearView Energy Partners, via the Associated Press

body.text: Ricardo Hausmann, a Harvard professor and a former Venezuelan planning minister, told the Associated Press that Venezuelans would not respect the deal and that no major US oil company would take it seriously, because they know it will not last. Democratic senators also criticised it: Tim Kaine of Virginia described it as corruption at epic scale, according to the same report. Oil market researcher Rory Johnston told Al Jazeera that the headline reserve figure is a red herring and that the terms that matter are still almost entirely unknown. The energy analyst Gregory Brew told Al Jazeera the arrangement was without precedent, and compared it to BP's claims over Iraqi and Iranian reserves before the Second World War, when the company was majority-owned by the British state.

The domestic backdrop in the United States is a high pump price. The average was about $4.09 a gallon on Friday, against $3.21 at the same point last year, and the country's strategic petroleum reserve fell below 300 million barrels in early August, down by more than 100 million since the start of 2026, according to Associated Press reports. Amy Myers Jaffe, who directs the Energy, Climate Justice and Sustainability Lab at New York University, told the agency the agreement would not change the retail price of petrol over the Labor Day weekend.

body.title: What is not established
items: Neither government has published the text of the agreement.
The two sides give different terms — 25 years in Caracas, 100-year development rights in Washington.
The private company that would hold the US stake has not been named.

uncertain: The duration of the agreement is reported two different ways: Rodriguez says 25 years, while US officials briefing the Associated Press describe 100-year development rights. Neither government has published the agreement, and no source consulted reconciles the two.
The private operator that would hold the US stake alongside the US government has not been named by either side.
How the 55 per cent 'effective output' figure breaks down between an equity stake and a right to purchase at cost has not been explained.

The $209 billion figure is characterised differently by different outlets: the Associated Press reports it as total projected tax revenue for Caracas from a Venezuelan government statement, Al Jazeera's Sunday report describes it as a possible annual value depending on oil prices, and agency copy carried by Daily Sabah gives more than $204 billion. This wire cannot say which is correct.
Venezuela's current daily oil production was not stated in any source consulted; the Associated Press says only that past output was more than 2.5 million barrels a day above the current level.
There is no published timeline for reaching the stated 1.5 million barrels a day target, and no statement of who pays for the infrastructure work needed to get there.
Whether any major US oil company will take part is unknown, and is disputed by at least one of the critics quoted.
Whether the agreement is valid under Venezuelan law, and whether a future Venezuelan government would honour it, is contested and unresolved.
Al Jazeera's report, published on Sunday 30 August, places Rodriguez's televised address on Saturday; the exact date and time of the address were not stated in the sources consulted.
No reaction from OPEC, from other oil producers, or from oil markets — closed for the weekend — was available in the sources consulted.
